def: The time from sending a request until the first output token arrives: network, queueing and prefill. It governs how quickly a response seems to start.
The average gap between output tokens after the first, set by the decode step time. End-to-end latency is TTFT plus (output tokens minus one) times TPOT.
The rate of completed requests that meet the latency objective (for example TTFT and TPOT targets). Unlike raw throughput, it falls when overloading makes requests too slow.
A workload whose speed is limited by how fast data can be read from memory rather than by arithmetic. Batch-1 decode is memory-bound.
FLOPs performed per byte moved to or from memory. It decides whether an operation is limited by memory bandwidth or by compute.
A chart and formula, attainable FLOP/s = min(peak compute, intensity times bandwidth), that shows which hardware limit binds a workload.
Scheduling at every decode step: finished sequences leave and waiting requests join immediately, keeping the batch full and cutting queue time.
Storing the KV cache in fixed-size blocks mapped by a block table, which nearly eliminates fragmentation and allows sharing of common prefixes.
In a stable system the average number of items in it equals arrival rate times average time in the system (L = lambda W). It links request rate, latency and concurrency.
Storing weights (or activations, or the KV cache) in fewer bits, with scales to map back to real values, to save memory and bandwidth at some cost in accuracy.
A post-training quantization method that rounds a layer's weights column by column and adjusts the remaining ones to cancel the output error, using calibration data.
Activation-aware weight quantization: it scales up the few weight channels that meet large activations before rounding so their relative error is smaller.
Reusing the stored KV cache of an identical prompt prefix so the server skips its prefill. It saves compute and TTFT but not decode time.
A cache that returns a stored answer when a new query's embedding is similar enough to a cached one. It saves a model call but risks false hits.
A cheap draft model proposes several tokens that the target model verifies in one pass, giving several tokens per pass with the target's exact output distribution.
The probability that a drafted token is accepted by the target model in speculative decoding. It sets the expected tokens per pass, (1 - a^(k+1)) / (1 - a).
Splitting each weight matrix across GPUs, with two all-reduces per transformer layer to combine partial results. It reduces per-token latency but needs fast links.
Assigning consecutive layers to different GPUs and passing activations between them. It needs little communication but does not lower per-token latency and has idle bubbles.
The fraction of a replica's saturated throughput you plan to run at peak, kept below 100% to leave headroom for bursts and latency.
